findings.claim: The unit calls its code 'pseudocode' throughout and never names the exam reference language, although every code block is already written in that language.
findings.truth: Code in the paper is presented in the exam reference language, and write or refine answers must use it or a high-level language. Two options: (a) an authoring pass adds a short paragraph to L2 naming the reference language and saying when it must be used, then relabels the 'pseudocode' wording in L7's file-handling section and in the L2, L6 and L7 question stems; (b) leave the content and rely on the exam-tip fix in F3. findings.claim: Required content from 2.2.3 is absent from all eleven lessons: SQL to search for data (SELECT, FROM, WHERE), basic string manipulation (concatenation and slicing) and random number generation.
findings.truth: All three sit in the spec's Required guidance and are examinable. No surgical edit can add them. Either extend L6 with string manipulation and L7 with SQL and random numbers, or build a twelfth lesson. Recommend extending L6 and L7, because a new lesson ripples into the podcast and video builds.

findings.claim: 'Functions such as int() and real() turn text into numbers'.
findings.truth: The published reference language uses float() for this cast; 'Real' is the data type name, not the function name. The reference-language guide is not in the spec markdown in this repo and could not be fetched, so the true value is unconfirmed. Low stakes either way, because minor syntax slips are not penalised.

findings.claim: The worked function uses 'squared' as both the function name and a local variable inside itself.
findings.truth: The traced output (16) is right and the code runs, but reusing the name is an anti-pattern that breaks in several high-level languages. Style only, so no edit.

summary: Eleven lessons checked. Every algorithm trace, truth table, DIV and MOD value, validation example and answer key was recomputed by hand and found correct. The mark-costing fault is the L2 exam tip telling students they may answer a 'write an algorithm' question in pseudocode or a flowchart, when such answers score nothing. The rest is exam-claim hygiene: three impossible 8-mark tariffs, seven questions carrying the other paper's question type, a copied definition in L3, an invented presentation-mark claim in L7 and a model answer that contradicts its own criterion. Two items need a judgement: the reference language is never named, and SQL, string manipulation and random numbers are missing from the unit.
